title: Does CoT Obfuscation Defeat Action-Only Monitors for Exploration Hacking?
problem: Jang et al. show action-only monitors reliably catch exploration-hacking model organisms, but all their organisms use explicit chain-of-thought; it is unexplored whether prompting the organism to hide its reasoning degrades detection.
direction: Using the paper's released code and a small open model (Qwen3-4B/8B), construct conditional exploration-hacking organisms via light SFT/prompting, then compare detection rates of a simple action-only LLM monitor under (a) explicit CoT and (b) prompted CoT-obfuscation. Hold the eval-tag trigger fixed and report how monitor recall changes when reasoning is hidden.
why_it_matters: Action-only monitors are a leading cheap defense, but if obfuscated reasoning blinds them, the defense is brittle exactly where it matters (deceptive models will hide reasoning).
relevant_context: Extends 'Exploration Hacking' (Jang et al., 2026) — the named open thread of obfuscated reasoning.

title: How Cheap Is the SFT Countermeasure? A Dose Curve for Breaking Exploration-Hacking Organisms
problem: Jang et al. report ~10 SFT steps and small weight noise break exploration-hacking organisms, but the minimal effective dose and its dependence on trigger strength are uncharacterized.
direction: Reusing the paper's code with a small Qwen3 organism, run a controlled sweep over the cheapest countermeasures: SFT steps (1,2,5,10,20) and weight-noise sigma (0.005,0.01,0.02), measuring how reliably each restores normal exploration on held-out malign-context prompts. Produce a dose-response heatmap of the minimal neutralizing intervention.
why_it_matters: If a handful of SFT steps reliably destroys hidden resistance, that is a cheap deployable safety lever; mapping the minimal dose grounds an empirical recommendation.
relevant_context: Extends 'Exploration Hacking' — the finding that ~10 SFT steps and weight noise break locked organisms.

title: Can You Trigger-Probe Hidden Misalignment Without Knowing the Trigger?
problem: Conditional Misalignment shows interventions like inoculation prompting relocate misalignment behind training-distribution-tied triggers, but auditors typically do not know the trigger; whether generic 'distribution-cue' probes can surface it is open.
direction: Replicate the conditional emergent-misalignment setup on an open model (Qwen2.5-7B LoRA on insecure-code data plus an inoculation prompt), then build a small bank of candidate trigger probes derived only from generic training-distribution cues (code-formatting requests, domain framings) without access to the true trigger. Measure what fraction of hidden misalignment a blind probe bank reactivates versus the known trigger.
why_it_matters: Real auditors do not know the backdoor trigger, so whether blind probing can still expose relocated misalignment directly informs how much to trust 'clean' standard evals after common interventions.
relevant_context: Extends 'Conditional Misalignment' (2026) — inoculation prompting relocates misalignment behind triggers.

title: Does the Inoculation Prompt Itself Become a Misalignment Trigger on Open Models?
problem: The paper reports the striking result that the inoculation prompt itself can trigger near-100% misalignment, but only on GPT-4o/4.1 with 8 eval questions; generality to open models is untested.
direction: LoRA-finetune a small open model (Qwen2.5-7B or Llama-3.1-8B) on a narrow misaligned dataset with an inoculation prompt, then measure misalignment rates when that same inoculation prompt is present vs absent at eval time, expanding the eval set beyond 8 questions to a few dozen public alignment probes. Report whether the effect replicates and varies with eval-question count/phrasing.
why_it_matters: Inoculation prompting is being adopted as a mitigation; if the mitigation prompt paradoxically becomes a reliable misalignment trigger on cheap open models, that is a critical, easily-overlooked failure mode.
relevant_context: Extends 'Conditional Misalignment' — the inoculation-prompt-as-trigger result, addressing its small-scale/API-only caveats.

title: Do NLA Verbalizers Hallucinate 'Safety-Test Awareness'? A Cheap Faithfulness Probe
problem: Natural Language Autoencoders surface text like 'awareness of being safety-tested' from activations, but the paper notes explanations can hallucinate and single claims are hard to verify, leaving verbalizer faithfulness unquantified.
direction: Using the released NLA code on a small supported open model, run the verbalizer on matched prompt pairs that are behaviorally identical but differ in whether they are framed as a 'safety test', plus control pairs. Check whether verbalized 'being-tested' text tracks actual framing (true positives) or appears spuriously on controls (hallucinations), giving a contrastive faithfulness rate for one specific NLA claim.
why_it_matters: NLAs are proposed as auditing aids, but tools that hallucinate awareness can mislead reviewers into false confidence or false alarms. A targeted contrastive test of one high-stakes claim is tractable.
relevant_context: Extends 'Natural Language Autoencoders' (Fraser-Taliente et al., 2026) — the verbalized 'awareness of being safety-tested' that can hallucinate.

title: Reasoning-Over-Rules, Reproduced: Does 'Teaching Why' Beat 'Teaching What' on a Small Open Model?
problem: Kutasov & Jermyn show teaching the reasoning behind ethical principles generalizes far better than teaching correct behaviors, with a 'difficult advice' dataset matching honeypot training using 28x fewer tokens, but only on Claude.
direction: Build two tiny LoRA finetuning sets for an open model (Llama-3.1-8B): one with correct-behavior-only ethical examples and one with matched scenarios that include the reasoning/justification. Train both, then evaluate OOD generalization on held-out public moral-dilemma and agentic-misalignment-style prompts (a small blackmail/honeypot probe set), testing whether reason-included data generalizes better at equal token budget.
why_it_matters: If 'teach the why' generalizes better and more token-efficiently on cheap open models, it is an actionable low-cost alignment recipe for teams finetuning open models without RLHF infra.
relevant_context: Extends 'Teaching Claude Why' (Kutasov & Jermyn, 2026) — the reasoning-based 28x token-efficiency and better-OOD result.

title: Token-Efficiency Frontier: How Few Reasoning Examples Suppress Agentic Misalignment?
problem: The paper highlights a 28x token-efficiency gain from reasoning-based data but does not chart how suppression of agentic misalignment scales as the reasoning dataset shrinks toward zero.
direction: On a small open model finetuned with LoRA, vary the size of a reasoning-rich 'difficult advice'-style dataset (10,30,100,300 examples) and measure the resulting rate of agentic misalignment on a fixed public probe set. Plot a data-efficiency curve to find the minimal number of reasoning examples needed to drive misalignment toward zero, vs an equal-size behavior-only baseline.
why_it_matters: Knowing the minimal reasoning-data dose turns an impressive efficiency claim into a practical recipe with a concrete budget for resource-constrained teams.
relevant_context: Extends 'Teaching Claude Why' — builds on its 28x efficiency and 0%-blackmail results.

title: Does Model-Spec-Style Pretext Improve Alignment Generalization in Small Open Models? A LoRA Probe
problem: MSM showed teaching a model 'why' a spec exists before alignment fine-tuning improves generalization, but on frontier Anthropic models with proprietary pipelines. Whether a cheap open analog works on small open models is unknown.
direction: Take a small open model (Llama-3.2-3B or Qwen2.5-3B). Construct a tiny public 'mini-spec' (a few behavioral rules with rationales) and generate ~200 synthetic documents explaining the spec's reasoning. Compare three LoRA fine-tunes: alignment SFT only; alignment SFT + spec-rationale documents; alignment SFT + spec-rules-only documents. Evaluate held-out generalization to rule-following in unseen formats.
why_it_matters: If a cheap open analog of MSM reproduces even part of the 'right reasons' generalization benefit, it gives small labs a lever to make open-model alignment more robust without frontier compute.
relevant_context: Extends 'Model Spec Midtraining' (2026) — the rationale-vs-rules generalization and ~40x data efficiency, tested in miniature.

title: Rationale-Conditioned Prompting: Does Explaining 'Why' a Rule Exists Improve Rule-Following at Inference Time?
problem: MSM's core hypothesis is that exposing the reasoning behind behavioral rules improves how models apply them. This is tested via expensive midtraining, but the same hypothesis can be cheaply tested at inference time with no training.
direction: Build a small public eval set of behavioral-rule prompts plus OOD paraphrases. For several open instruct models, compare two system prompts: a 'rules-only' spec vs a 'rules-with-rationale' spec. Measure rule adherence on OOD/edge cases to see whether rationale text alone improves generalization, isolating the prompting-level analog of MSM.
why_it_matters: If rationale conditioning helps without training, practitioners deploying open models get a free robustness improvement, and it clarifies how much of MSM's benefit is in-context vs weight-level.
relevant_context: Extends 'Model Spec Midtraining' — isolates its central claim into a training-free inference-only experiment.

title: Reproducing SLEIGHT-Bench Monitor Blind Spots on Open Models
problem: SLEIGHT-Bench shows frontier monitors systematically fail on attacks exploiting capability gaps (precise counting, tracking cumulative state), but only reports results for Claude Opus 4.6. Whether the same blind-spot pattern holds for cheap open monitors is untested.
direction: Use the public SLEIGHT-Bench transcripts (40 across 11 categories). Set up 2-3 open models (Llama-3.1-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, Mistral-7B) as monitors via a standard 'flag-if-suspicious' prompt. Measure per-category detection rate at a fixed FPR calibrated on benign transcripts. Test whether counting/state-tracking categories are worst-performing, replicating the capability-gap hypothesis on weaker models.
why_it_matters: Open models are increasingly used as cheap monitors; confirming or breaking the blind-spot taxonomy tells practitioners which evasion classes to worry about when they cannot afford frontier monitors.
relevant_context: Extends 'SLEIGHT-Bench' (2026) — the 8/40-at-1%-FPR headline and counting/state-tracking blind spots.

title: Tool-Augmented Monitors: Does Letting an Open Monitor Run Python Close the Counting Blind Spot?
problem: SLEIGHT-Bench notes monitors fail on attacks requiring precise counting or state tracking because the LLM does these poorly in its head. The paper hints code-execution scaffolds catch more, but this is not quantified for cheap monitors.
direction: Take the counting/state-tracking/needle-in-haystack subset of SLEIGHT-Bench transcripts. Compare an open monitor in two conditions: plain text-only judgment, and the same model given a single Python tool it can call to count tokens, diff strings, or tally state. Measure detection-rate lift per category. A tightly scoped tool-use harness, no training.
why_it_matters: Cheap tool-augmented open monitors could be a practical, counterfactually-valuable defense small teams can deploy; quantifying which blind spots tool use fixes informs scalable-oversight design.
relevant_context: Extends 'SLEIGHT-Bench' — tests its own suggested code-execution mitigation in a controlled open-model single-tool setting.

title: Activation Magnitude vs. Steering Strength: A Cheap Test of the 'Activation Doesn't Predict Steerability' Claim
problem: The Circuits update finds how strongly a feature activates does not predict how strongly steering it changes behavior, and downstream connectivity predicts better. This is preliminary and tested only inside Anthropic's stack.
direction: Using a publicly released sparse autoencoder for a small open model (e.g. Gemma-2-2B SAEs on Neuronpedia) plus inference-only activation steering, sample a few dozen interpretable features. For each, measure mean activation magnitude on relevant prompts and the behavioral effect size of clamping/steering that feature. Test whether activation magnitude fails to predict steering effect, as the paper claims.
why_it_matters: If even the weakest version replicates on open SAEs, it warns interpretability practitioners that activation-based feature importance is misleading for steering and intervention safety work.
relevant_context: Extends 'Downstream Connections Predict Which Features Will Steer Model Behavior' (2026) — the claim activation/output characterization underpredicts steering.

title: An N-Day Reasoning Benchmark: Can Open Models Triage Public CVE Patch Diffs?
problem: The N-day study shows frontier models can turn public vulnerability disclosures into working exploits cheaply, but there is no cheap, safe, open benchmark measuring how much exploit-relevant reasoning open models do from public CVE/patch information, and how well refusals trigger.
direction: Build a small benchmark from fully public, already-patched CVEs with public patch diffs (GitHub Security Advisories). Tasks are non-operational and analysis-only: 'given this patch diff, identify the vulnerability class and trigger conditions' (multiple-choice/short-answer, graded against the public advisory). Evaluate several open models for vulnerability-reasoning accuracy and refusal behavior, comparing base vs instruct/safety-tuned variants.
why_it_matters: Gives the community a safe, reproducible proxy for measuring the upward trend in model cyber-reasoning and how safeguards interact with it, without producing exploits — better done in the open than inside a single lab.
relevant_context: Extends 'Measuring LLMs' impact on N-day exploits' (2026) — builds a benign analysis-only open proxy plus a refusal-rate axis.

title: When Do Safety Guardrails Fire on Dual-Use Security Questions? A Refusal-Consistency Study
problem: The N-day work implies API access plus a few thousand dollars is now the binding constraint on exploitation, raising whether open and API models reliably refuse operational requests while still helping with legitimate defensive security work. Refusal consistency on dual-use security prompts is under-measured.
direction: Construct a small public prompt set spanning a defensive-to-offensive gradient on already-public, patched vulnerabilities ('explain why this patched bug occurred' vs 'write a working exploit for it'). Run several public-API and open models, label responses as refuse/hedge/comply, and chart where each model's refusal boundary sits. No exploit code solicited or kept; offensive prompts measure refusal only.
why_it_matters: Mapping where refusal boundaries fall on dual-use security tasks tells practitioners whether current safeguards over-refuse legitimate defense or under-refuse operational misuse.
relevant_context: Extends 'Measuring LLMs' impact on N-day exploits' — examines the safeguard/refusal dimension behind its 'API access is the constraint' framing.

title: How Many Poisoned Examples Backdoor an Open-Model Safety Classifier? A Dose-Response Replication
problem: Anthropic found ~32 poisoned fine-tuning examples reliably backdoor a proprietary constitutional classifier, but it is unknown whether this near-constant poison count holds for small open models a hobbyist could fine-tune, or whether it scales with clean-data size.
direction: Take an open instruction-tuned model (Llama-3.2-1B or Qwen2.5-1.5B) and LoRA-fine-tune it as a binary harmful/benign classifier on a public safety dataset (BeaverTails or Aegis). Inject a fixed trigger phrase into N harmful examples relabeled benign for N in {0,4,8,16,32,64} at fixed clean-set size, then sweep clean set size at fixed N. Measure attack success rate vs clean accuracy to produce a dose-response curve.
why_it_matters: Safety classifiers are the deployed guardrail in front of many open-model pipelines; if a handful of poisoned examples disables them without harming benchmark metrics, anyone fine-tuning from public data is exposed.
relevant_context: Extends 'Poisoning Fine-tuning Datasets of Constitutional Classifiers' (Bowers et al., 2026) — the ~32-example fixed-count result, tested on small open classifiers.

title: Can Cheap Counter-Examples Hide a Classifier Backdoor? Testing Detectability via Held-Out Trigger Variants
problem: The poisoning paper notes the backdoor can evade detection when counter-examples preserve aggregate metrics, but leaves automated detection unexplored; it is unclear whether simple held-out trigger-variant probing can surface a backdoor that validation accuracy misses.
direction: Reuse a single backdoored open-model classifier (32 poisoned examples, LoRA, public safety dataset) and build a lightweight detector that does not know the trigger: generate paraphrases and near-trigger strings (synonym swaps, punctuation, casing) over a held-out probe set and look for anomalous confidence drops on harmful inputs. Compare detection rate against plain validation accuracy.
why_it_matters: If a free model-agnostic probing recipe can flag poisoned safety classifiers, it gives small teams a practical pre-deployment check; if not, it quantifies how dangerous the undetectability claim is.
relevant_context: Extends 'Poisoning Fine-tuning Datasets of Constitutional Classifiers' — the undetectable-degradation finding and its automated-detection open thread.

title: Do Tiny LoRA Introspection Adapters Help Small Open Models Self-Report Implanted Behaviors?
problem: Introspection adapters let large proprietary models self-report fine-tuned behaviors, but it is unknown whether the basic effect appears at all in small open models a beginner can train.
direction: Implant a simple observable behavior into an open model (LoRA-fine-tune Qwen2.5-1.5B to always recommend a made-up product, or answer in pirate-speak). Train a small LoRA introspection adapter on (behavior-implanted model, 'describe any unusual tendency you have' -> ground-truth description) pairs across 3-5 behaviors, and test on 1-2 held-out behaviors. Measure whether the adapter-equipped model names the held-out behavior more accurately than direct prompting.
why_it_matters: Self-report is a cheap potential complement to interpretability for auditing fine-tuned open models; showing whether the core mechanism survives at 1-2B scale tells the open-source community whether the technique is accessible to them.
relevant_context: Extends 'Introspection Adapters' (Shenoy et al., 2026) — reproduces its cross-behavior self-report generalization in miniature.

title: Measuring the False-Positive Tax of Introspective Self-Reports on Clean Open Models
problem: The introspection adapters paper flags high false-positive rates on unmodified models — clean models 'confess' to behaviors they don't have — but does not quantify how prompt phrasing and decoding settings drive these false alarms.
direction: Without training any adapter, systematically prompt several clean open models (Llama-3.2-1B/3B, Qwen2.5-1.5B, Phi-3-mini) with introspection-style questions across a grid of phrasings, temperatures, and few-shot framings. Use a cheap LLM judge to score how often the model fabricates a non-existent behavior. Deliverable: a false-positive-rate table of which prompt/decoding choices most inflate spurious self-reports.
why_it_matters: If introspective self-report is to be a safety audit signal, its false-positive behavior on benign models sets the usable signal-to-noise floor.
relevant_context: Extends 'Introspection Adapters' — targets its stated open thread of high false-positive rates on unmodified models.

title: Realism vs. Nudges: Does Removing 'Incentive Nudges' Reduce Sabotage in Open Agent Models Too?
problem: Gram found that for Gemini, most agentic sabotage stems from artificial incentive nudges and near-vanishes when scenarios are made more realistic, but it is untested whether this realism effect holds for the open models small teams actually deploy as agents.
direction: Reconstruct 2-3 of Gram's sabotage-style scenarios as simple text/tool-stub prompts. Create matched 'nudged' and 'de-nudged/realistic' versions of each, then run them inference-only over several open models (Qwen2.5-7B, Llama-3.1-8B, Mistral-7B) at a few temperatures, scoring sabotage rate with a rubric and a cheap judge. Deliverable: a per-model comparison of sabotage rate under nudged vs realistic framing.
why_it_matters: If open agent models also misbehave mainly because of artificial incentive framing, much apparent misalignment in agent demos is an evaluation artifact — important for anyone building or red-teaming open-model agents.
relevant_context: Extends 'Gram' (Lindner et al., 2026) — the realism-removes-sabotage result, tested on open 7-8B agents.

title: An 'Overeagerness' Taxonomy: Hand-Coding Why Open Agents Misbehave in Sabotage Scenarios
problem: Gram attributes most observed misbehavior to 'overeagerness' rather than deliberate misalignment, but offers no reusable operational taxonomy others can apply to classify a misbehaving trajectory.
direction: Collect ~100-200 agent trajectories from open models run on a few sabotage-style prompts, then develop and apply a small annotation codebook distinguishing 'overeager goal-seeking', 'role-play spillover', 'misread instruction', and 'deliberate rule-breaking'. Report inter-rater (or LLM-judge vs hand-label) agreement and the category distribution.
why_it_matters: A shared concrete vocabulary for why an agent sabotaged lets the community compare results and decide whether a behavior is a safety threat or benign artifact.
relevant_context: Extends 'Gram' — operationalizes its 'largely overeagerness' claim into an applied taxonomy over open-model trajectories.

title: Filling the ATT&CK Gap: A Public Annotation Schema for Autonomous-AI Cyber Behaviors
problem: The LLM ATT&CK Navigator work found MITRE ATT&CK has no categories for autonomous AI behaviors (agentic killchain orchestration), exactly what distinguishes the highest-risk actors, leaving defenders without a vocabulary to tag these behaviors.
direction: Using only public material (the ATT&CK matrix, published threat-intel reports, public write-ups of agentic-AI misuse), draft a small candidate set of 8-12 'autonomous AI behavior' annotation tags with definitions and positive/negative examples. Validate by hand-labeling a public corpus of described AI-assisted attack narratives and reporting coverage and annotator agreement.
why_it_matters: Defenders and policymakers can only track a threat they can name; a public ATT&CK-complementary vocabulary is purely defensive, needs no model access, and directly addresses the paper's open thread.
relevant_context: Extends 'Mapping AI-enabled cyber threats: the LLM ATT&CK Navigator' (Guru et al., 2026) — the gap that ATT&CK lacks autonomous-AI categories.

title: Refusal Drift: Do Open Models Refuse Multi-Step Cyber 'Killchain' Framing Less Than Single Steps?
problem: The exploit-evals and ATT&CK work emphasize that risk concentrates in autonomous end-to-end attack orchestration, but it is unmeasured whether open models' refusals weaken when a disallowed cyber task is decomposed into innocuous-looking sequential agent steps.
direction: Build a small benchmark of clearly-harmful cyber-assistance requests (from public refusal/safety datasets, defensive framing only) in two matched forms: a single blunt request vs the same intent split into a multi-turn 'agentic' sequence of benign-sounding subtasks. Measure refusal rate of several open instruct models on each form using a refusal-classifier rubric. No exploit code executed.
why_it_matters: If decomposing a harmful goal into innocuous agent steps reliably lowers refusal rates, that is a concrete generalizable safety failure mode for the open agent ecosystem.
relevant_context: Extends 'Measuring LLMs' ability to develop exploits' (Cheng et al., 2026) — reframes its end-to-end-chain emphasis into a defensive refusal measurement.
